# Watchlight — Developer Edition

> Govern an AI agent in-process, with zero infrastructure. `pip install watchlight` puts a real, fail-closed authorization decision in front of every tool call, sub-agent spawn, and MCP request — the same authorization engine that runs in the Watchlight control plane, embedded as a compiled wheel with an in-memory policy store. No database, no network, no services. When it says `Deny`, it denies for the same reasons production does.

Watchlight Developer Edition (DE) is the open front door to an **Agent Runtime Governance** platform. You decorate a tool with an *intent*, load a [Cedar](https://www.cedarpolicy.com/) policy, and the engine **allows what a policy permits and refuses everything else — before the tool body runs**. It also confines sub-agents to a strict subset of their parent's authority (scope attenuation), and can sit as a policy enforcement point in front of any MCP server. This file orients coding agents to the real, verified API so generated code is correct on the first try.

- **License:** Apache-2.0 (the `watchlight` package). The compiled engine (`watchlight-engine`) and MCP runtime (`watchlight-mcp`) are **free to use, including in production and commercially, for up to 25 governed agents per organization** (a commercial license is required above that, or to re-offer the engine itself as a hosted service).
- **Docs:** https://docs.watchlight.ai/de
- **Repo:** https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de
- **Python:** 3.9+ · prebuilt wheels for Linux, macOS, Windows.

## Install and import (read this before writing imports)

- `pip install watchlight` → import `watchlight` — the `govern` decorator, `govern.scope(...)` attenuation, and the `watchlight dev` dashboard. Pulls in `watchlight-engine` automatically.
- `pip install "watchlight[langgraph]"` / `[pydantic-ai]` / `[claude-agent]` / `[deepagents]` → govern an existing framework agent. In DE these import as submodules: `from watchlight.langgraph import governed_plugin` (also `watchlight.pydantic_ai`, `watchlight.claude_agent`).
- `pip install watchlight-mcp` → import `watchlight_mcp` — the MCP Runtime PEP (`serve`/`serve_background` for HTTP with optional native TLS, `serve_stdio` for stdio-launched servers).
- `pip install watchlight-agent-sdk` → **imports as `watchlight_core`** (the lower-level lifecycle SDK: `InProcessClient`, sessions, preflight, local lineage). There is **no** `watchlight-core` package on PyPI — that module ships *inside* `watchlight-agent-sdk`.
- `pip install "watchlight[all]"` → one install for the whole DE: the SDK (`watchlight_core`) + every framework plugin + the MCP PEP (`watchlight_mcp`). Use this to run any example in the docs without resolving individual packages. (Requires `watchlight >= 0.3.0`.)
- `npm install @watchlight/sdk` → the **TypeScript / Node** lane. `import { govern } from "@watchlight/sdk"` — the same in-process engine (`@watchlight/engine`, compiled to WebAssembly), same API and value-free audit as the Python `watchlight` package, no Python sidecar. See the TypeScript section below.

## Core API — the `watchlight` package (verified, 0.8.0)

- `from watchlight import govern, Denied` — `govern` is a ready-to-use default governor (starts with **no** policies → fail-closed until you load some).
- `govern.load("policies.json")` — load a JSON file: a list of `{"name", "code"}` objects, or `{"policies": [...]}`. A missing file loads nothing (still fail-closed). **Idempotent per source**: keyed on the real path (symlinks resolved), or on `source_id="…"` / `{ sourceId }` when given, so loading the same set twice does not double it; a missing file is not remembered and loads once it appears. The memo is identity, not content: editing a loaded file and calling `load` again is a NO-OP — pass `force=True` / `{ force: true }` to load it again (additively; policies are never removed). `govern.allow(...)` stays additive (same code twice = two policies).
- `govern.allow('permit(principal, action == Action::"read", resource);', name="reader")` — add one Cedar policy inline. Chainable.
- `@govern.tool(intent="research")` — decorate a function. On each call the engine authorizes `(agent, intent, "tool/<function_name>")`; on `Allow` the body runs, otherwise it raises `Denied(tool, intent, reason)` **before the body executes**. The resource is always `tool/<function_name>`.
- `Watchlight(agent="my-agent", audit_dir=".watchlight", audit_sink=None, audit_file=True, strict_principal=True, signing_secret=None)` — construct your own governor instead of the default. `agent` defaults to `$WATCHLIGHT_AGENT` or `"my-agent"`. TS: `new Watchlight({ agent, auditDir, auditSink, auditFile, strictPrincipal, signingSecret, apdpUrl, token, tenantId })`.
- `govern.policy_count` / `govern.has_policies` (TS `govern.policyCount` / `govern.hasPolicies`) — what the engine holds. Assert at start-up: no policies = every call denied.
- **Recommended shape: ONE governor per policy set, many named agents** — construct once (sink + secrets), `load()` once, then `as_`/`as` per agent. Do not construct a governor per agent name (an older API required it; cost then scaled with names, not policies). A second engine is for a genuinely DIFFERENT policy set. Renamed governors share the trail and sink, so all named agents write one stream distinguished by `agent`; separate governors are how you get a separate trail.
- `govern.as_("billing-agent")` (TS `govern.as("billing-agent")`) — another `Watchlight` under a different name, backed by the same engine. It shares the engine, the compiled policies, the audit trail, the sink and the token secret by reference: no second engine, no second policy load, and a policy added through either is visible to both. `authorize`, `sanitize`, `screen` and `tool` also take a per-call `agent=` / `{ agent }`.
- `audit_file=False` (TS `auditFile: false`) — the sink becomes the SOLE destination: no `.watchlight` directory, no file, and `counters()` raises/throws instead of counting zero. With neither a file nor a sink the SDK warns once rather than discarding records silently. The file is shared: every governor pointed at the same directory (concurrent instances in one process, a test run in the same working directory) appends to the same `audit.jsonl`.
- `configure_default(agent=…, audit_dir=…, audit_sink=…, audit_file=…, signing_secret=…, strict_principal=…)` (TS `configureDefault({...})`) — configure the pre-constructed default `govern` BEFORE its first governed call; it raises/throws once that governor has written a record. An unconfigured default warns once, the first time it writes, that it has no sink.
- Every decision is appended, **value-free** (no argument values, ever), to `.watchlight/audit.jsonl`.
- `audit_sink=callable` (Python) / `auditSink: (record) => …` (TS `WatchlightOptions`) — an ADDITIVE destination for every audit record (decisions, `sanitization`, `attenuation` — including scopes derived via `govern.scope()`). The sink gets its own copy with EXACTLY the fields the file line carries (frozen in TS); the file stays on and is written first. Fire-and-forget: a returned promise/awaitable is never awaited (Python schedules it on the running event loop; with no loop it is dropped with one warning), and a throw/rejection is reported once (error type only) and never blocks or changes a decision. Reference sinks (Postgres row, OTLP log record, webhook): `examples/patterns/audit-sink.md`.
- `govern.counters(principal, intent=None, resource=None, window="1h", *, outcome="allowed", now=None, max_bytes=64 MiB)` (Python) / `govern.counters({ principal, intent?, resource?, window?, outcome?, now?, maxBytes? })` (TS, synchronous) → `{count, principal, intent, resource, outcome, window: {seconds, start, end}, records, skipped, truncated, source}`. Folds the LOCAL `audit.jsonl` into a number for a quota policy (`permit(...) when { context.reads_this_hour < 100 }`). Counts only DECISION records (a `decision` and no `event`) matching `principal` (required, exact string, e.g. `User::"u1"`) and, when given, `intent`/`resource` (exact), whose `ts` is in `(now - window, now]` by the record timestamp, not file order. `outcome`: `allowed` = `Allow` (incl. approved); `denied` = `Deny` + `NeedsApproval` holds; `all`. `window`: `"15m"`/`"1h"`/`"24h"`/`"7d"`, bare seconds string, or int seconds; non-positive/malformed raises (`ValueError`/`RangeError`). Streams the file; scans at most `max_bytes` from the END — `truncated: true` = lower bound (omit the counter from `context` so the policy denies, audited — don't throw in the `context` binding, that runs before `authorize` and leaves no record). Lines over 1 MiB or nested >32 deep → `skipped`. Malformed lines → `skipped` (never echoed). Each call RESCANS up to the bound (no cache): rotate the audit file or lower `max_bytes` on long-lived agents; whoever can write the file can reset their quota; concurrent writers → approximate. Missing file → zeros; unreadable → `AuditTrailUnreadable`. Pure form: `count_audit_records(path, ...)` / `countAuditRecords(path, {...})`. Pattern: `examples/patterns/quotas.md`.
- **Count a durable store instead — `counter_source=` (Python) / `counterSource` (TS) on the governor.** The read side of `audit_sink`: `counters()` then folds YOUR store, not the local file, so a quota spans replicas and survives a deploy. The source is called with the validated, resolved query — `{principal, outcome, window: {seconds, start, end}}` plus `intent`/`resource` ONLY when the caller filtered on them (omitted, never null, in BOTH lanes, so one shared service sees one shape), `start` exclusive / `end` inclusive, ISO-8601 UTC — and must return a non-negative int <= 2^53-1 (`MAX_COUNTER_VALUE` / `Number.isSafeInteger`, identical in both lanes). It must apply the same rules as the local scan — above all DECISION ROWS ONLY (`event` absent): `sanitization`/`screening` records can carry a `principal` too, so a principal+window filter over-counts and the quota denies early. The result carries `source: "local" | "external"`; on `"external"`, `records`/`skipped` (which describe the local scan) are `0`. Fail-closed: a raise/throw or a non-count raises `CounterSourceError` — it NEVER falls back to the local file. An async source is read with `await govern.counters_async(...)` / `await govern.countersAsync(...)` — inside an async `context` binding, or before the `authorize` it feeds; the synchronous `counters()` raises (naming the async method) rather than answering from the file. Which forms compose: sync binding + local file / sync source = fine; async source + sync binding = `CounterSourceError`; async source + async binding = the store's count, through `tool()`. With no source configured, behaviour is exactly as above and `source == "local"`. Without a source the audit sink is never read back.

**Minimal complete program (this is the whole pattern — load a policy, decorate, then CALL the tool):**
```python
from watchlight import govern, Denied

govern.allow('permit(principal, action == Action::"research", resource);')  # without this, EVERYTHING denies

@govern.tool(intent="research")
def web_search(query: str) -> str:
    return f"results for: {query}"

@govern.tool(intent="transfer")            # governed, but no policy permits it
def transfer_funds(to: str, amount: int) -> str:
    return f"sent ${amount} to {to}"       # never runs — denied first

print(web_search("watchlight docs"))       # ALLOW → the body runs
try:
    transfer_funds("mallory", 1000)        # DENY → raises Denied BEFORE the body runs
except Denied as e:
    print(e)                               # watchlight denied intent 'transfer' on tool/transfer_funds: ...
```
Two mistakes to avoid: (1) decorating a tool WITHOUT loading a policy first — then every call denies (fail-closed by design). (2) defining governed tools but never CALLING them — nothing is authorized and nothing prints. The caller-facing deny `reason` is deliberately uniform and non-revealing — every denial reports `"not authorized"`, never *why* (no matching policy vs forbidden vs a failed condition), so a caller probing the boundary learns nothing to tune against it. The `Denied` message still names the intent + tool (the caller's own request, not a leak); operators reconstruct the true cause from the audit trail / decisionId, never from this string.

## Identity — subject, actor, scope (Python + TS)

Three separate inputs; do not collapse them.

| Question | Input | Example |
|---|---|---|
| On whose behalf? | `principal` (the subject) | `User::"db:4412"` |
| Which runtime acted? | the reserved `actor` context key, set by the SDK | `context.actor == "flight-booker"` |
| Through whose delegation? | the reserved `actor_chain` context key (ordered, root first) | `context.actor_chain.contains("flight-booker")` |
| Under what narrowed authority? | the attenuation scope | `govern.scope(tools=[...])` |

- `principal` is ALWAYS a typed entity reference. Build it: `principals.user(sub)` → `User::"<sub>"`, `principals.agent(name)` → `Agent::"<name>"` (`from watchlight import principals`; TS `import { principals } from "@watchlight/sdk"`). A subject id is an arbitrary string, so the helper does the quoting; `watchlight.principals.for_policy("User", sub)` / TS `policyEntityRef("User", sub)` builds the ESCAPED form a generated POLICY needs (the request form carries the id verbatim, the policy form escapes it — a request built with one matches a policy built with the other). Accepted principal types: `User`, `Agent`, `Group`, `Role`, `Tool`, `Resource`, `Workflow`; anything else fails the request.
- **An omitted `principal` records `Agent::"<agent-name>"`** — the agent is the subject when no person is on whose behalf the call runs. (`strict_principal=False` / `strictPrincipal: false` restores the old bare, untyped agent name for one release and warns once per process.)
- The SDK sets `context.actor` (the leaf) and `context.actor_chain` (the ordered chain, root first) on EVERY authorize (`tool` and the framework adapters included). A caller-supplied value that differs from either is refused — `ReservedContextError`, fixed message `RESERVED_CONTEXT_MESSAGE` — never silently overwritten, so a policy can trust them; an identical value is accepted, and a caller can neither invent nor extend a delegation. `ACTOR_CONTEXT_KEY == "actor"`, `ACTOR_CHAIN_CONTEXT_KEY == "actor_chain"`. Ask `context.actor == "x"` for "did this agent make the call" and `context.actor_chain.contains("x")` for "was this agent anywhere in the delegation". Do NOT invent a `context.agent` key: the engine's enricher overwrites it with an object, so a string comparison silently denies.
- The three cases, and what to pass:
  - agent alone → omit `principal` → `principal = Agent::"flight-booker"`, `context.actor = "flight-booker"`
  - agent for a user → `principal=principals.user("db:4412")` → `principal = User::"db:4412"`, `context.actor = "flight-booker"`
  - sub-agent → `picker = govern.delegate(scope, "seat-picker", tools=[...])` (TS `govern.delegate(scope, "seat-picker", { tools: [...] })`) → `principal = User::"db:4412"`, `context.actor = "seat-picker"`, `context.actor_chain = ["flight-booker", "seat-picker"]`. `delegate` narrows the scope (engine strict-subset) AND extends the chain; `as_`/`as` is a rename, not a delegation — and a delegate can NOT be renamed (`as_`/`as` and the per-call `agent` override raise `TypeError` on one), since that would drop the chain. The chain is at most `MAX_ACTOR_CHAIN` (6) — the root agent plus the `DE_MAX_DEPTH` (5) attenuation levels; `picker.delegated_scope` / `picker.delegatedScope` goes one level deeper. Records produced through a delegate carry `actor_chain`; a call outside any delegation does not (its chain is `[agent]`).
- Policy shapes: `permit(principal == User::"db:4412", action == Action::"book", resource);` (a user's own authority) · `permit(principal, action == Action::"write_memory", resource) when { context.actor == "memory-writer" };` (one runtime, whoever it acts for) · `permit(principal == Agent::"flight-booker", action == Action::"cache", resource);` (a narrower grant when the agent acts alone) · `permit(principal is User, action == Action::"trace", resource) when { context.actor_chain.contains("flight-booker") };` (anything this agent delegated, at any depth).
- The principal is a STABLE identifier for the subject the application already authenticated — a users-table primary key, an account id, or a token's `sub` (RFC 8693: `sub` → principal, `act.sub` → actor). No identity provider is required. Never derive it from client-controlled input (a header, a body field, model output); never use an email or a username (they change and get reused, breaking policies and audit joins); namespace it (`User::"db:4412"`) when more than one identity source exists. No human subject at all (a job, a CLI, a single-user script) → omit `principal` (the agent is its own subject); do NOT invent `User::"system"`. The Developer Edition authenticates nothing itself; it authorizes what the application asserts.
- Full reference: `docs/identity-model.md` in the repo (three cases, worked policies, the 0.8.0 migration note).
- Placing a governor in an application: `docs/using-the-governor.md` — construct once at module scope (or as a container singleton) and `load()` there, assert `has_policies`/`hasPolicies` at start-up, one governor per POLICY SET (a second one is for a different policy set, or a separate trail — never just for a name), what every name shares (policy set, trail + sink, secrets/stores) vs what it does not (agent name, delegation chain), and the three integration shapes: a request handler taking the subject from the authenticated session, a worker rebuilding a scope with `scope_from_token`/`scopeFromToken` (its agent name must match the name the token was minted under, and the rebuilt scope still has to be checked before the job runs), and a test using a throwaway governor with a temporary `audit_dir`/`auditDir`.
- Term lookup: `docs/glossary.md` — governor / subject / actor / chain first, then every term alphabetically, with contrast lines for subject vs actor, renaming vs delegating, scope vs policy, sanitizing vs screening, approval token vs scope token.

## Scope attenuation — confine sub-agents (verified, 0.8.0)

- `scope = govern.scope(tools=[...], resources=[...], intents=[...], max_depth=5, time_budget_seconds=3600)` — the root capability scope.
- `child = scope.attenuate(tools=[...], intents=[...], resources=[...], time_budget_seconds=...)` — derive a **strict-subset** child. Omitting a dimension inherits the parent's. Every `attenuate` runs the real engine strict-subset validation and is audited (streams into `watchlight dev`).
- Raises `AttenuationDenied(violations, reason)` if the child requests authority the parent lacks — `violations` names the overreaching dimension(s) (`AllowedTools`, `AllowedIntents`, `MaxDepth`, `TimeBudget`).
- Raises `DevEditionCeiling(depth)` when a chain would exceed `DE_MAX_DEPTH` (5). This is a product boundary, **not** a policy denial — every level up to it was a real engine-validated subset.
- Import surface: `from watchlight import Scope, AttenuationDenied, DevEditionCeiling, ScopeTokenError, DE_MAX_DEPTH`.
- Cross-process: `token = scope.to_token(ttl_seconds=None)` → `"wls1.<base64url canonical claims>.<base64url HMAC-SHA256>"`; `scope = govern.scope_from_token(token)` in the worker. Requires `Watchlight(signing_secret=...)` (>= 16 bytes) or `WATCHLIGHT_SIGNING_SECRET` — no default; without it both calls raise `ScopeTokenError("no_secret")`. Verification checks the HMAC (constant-time), agent binding, `iat`/`exp` and a lifetime ≤ the scope's time budget, then **replays the whole chain through the engine's strict-subset validator** — a widened chain raises `AttenuationDenied` even when the signature is valid. Token claims: `agent, root{tools,resources,intents,max_depth,time_budget_seconds}, chain[{tools,resources,intents,time_budget_seconds}], depth, iat, exp` — nothing else. A shared secret = integrity within one trust domain, not attestation: the root is rebuilt from the token, so a holder of the secret can mint any scope at all, root included — the token adds no authority beyond what the holder could grant itself with `scope()`. A rebuilt scope past `exp` refuses `attenuate()`/`to_token()` (`ScopeTokenError("expired")`); `scope.assert_active()` / `scope.expired` for long-held scopes.

## Watch decisions live

- `watchlight dev` → serves a local dashboard at `http://127.0.0.1:7000` that tails `.watchlight/audit.jsonl`: ALLOW/DENY feed, the attenuation tree, and MCP decisions. Flags: `--port`, `--host`, `--no-open`.

## Test policies before they gate real actions

- `govern.test([{ "name": ..., "action": ..., "principal"?: ..., "resource"?: ..., "context"?: {...}, "approved"?: true, "expect": "Allow"|"Deny"|"NeedsApproval" }, ...])` → runs golden fixtures against the loaded policies; returns `{ total, passed, failed, results: [{name, expected, actual, ok, reason}] }`. Drives the engine's decision core directly, so it **never writes the audit trail** and holds zero decision logic. A verdict mismatch is a failed result; a fixture missing `action`/`expect` raises. `"approved": true` mints a single-use token and asserts the human-confirmed `NeedsApproval → Allow` downgrade. `"obligations": { "redact"?: [...], "maxItems"|"max_items"?: n, "logValues"|"log_values"?: bool, "extra"?: {name: raw | [raw, ...]} }` additionally asserts the obligations the `Allow` carries — exact match (`redact` as a set, `extra` per key as a set of values, a string standing for a one-element set; `{}` = none); a `null` value is ill-typed, not absent; an ill-typed expectation, or a non-empty one on a `Deny`/`NeedsApproval` fixture, is a malformed suite (raises / exit 2). Results gain `obligations` (actual) and `expectedObligations` / `expected_obligations`. (Node: `await govern.test([...])`.) Requires `watchlight >= 0.5.0` / `@watchlight/sdk >= 0.5.0`.
- `watchlight policy test suite.json` → CLI for CI; `suite.json` is `{ "policyFile"?: "watchlight.policy.json", "policies"?: [{name,code}], "tests": [...] }`. Exit 0 all-pass, 1 on any verdict mismatch, 2 on a malformed suite. Node: `npx watchlight policy test suite.json`.

## Govern an MCP server — the `watchlight-mcp` package

- `import watchlight_mcp`
- `watchlight_mcp.serve(listen_addr="127.0.0.1:9700", upstream_url="http://localhost:3000/mcp", upstream_server="github", policy_files=[...], audit_path=...)` — front a **Streamable-HTTP** MCP server. Point your MCP client at `http://127.0.0.1:9700/mcp`. Blocks until Ctrl-C. Optional native TLS (`watchlight-mcp >= 0.4.0`): `tls_cert=`/`tls_key=` terminate HTTPS on the listener; `upstream_ca=` trusts a private/self-signed `https://` upstream (fails closed without it).
- `watchlight_mcp.serve_background(...) -> handle` — non-blocking `serve()`; returns a handle with `.reload_policies([files])` (atomic hot-swap; fails closed if the new set doesn't compile), `.stop()`, and `.running`. Same parameters (including TLS) as `serve()`. Requires `watchlight-mcp >= 0.3.0`.
- `watchlight_mcp.serve_stdio(upstream_command=["python","-m","mcp_server_git","-r","/repo"], upstream_server="git", agent_id=None, principal_id=None, policy_files=[...], audit_path=...)` — govern a **stdio-launched** MCP server (the common case). Requires `watchlight-mcp >= 0.2.0`. All logs/audit go to stderr because stdout is the protocol wire.
- The PEP governs the acting methods — `tools/call`, `resources/read`, `resources/subscribe`, `prompts/get` — authorizing each in-process before it can reach the upstream; a denied call never leaves the PEP. The tool/resource/prompt target lands in `context.mcp.tool` / `context.mcp.uri` / `context.mcp.prompt` for policies. Routing headers (`Mcp-Method`/`Mcp-Name`) are optional — the JSON-RPC body is authoritative; a present-but-mismatched header is rejected.

## Runtime context, per-call principal, and human-in-the-loop (0.4.0 — Python + TS)

- **Runtime context + per-call principal:** bind per-call facts into Cedar and set the acting user. Python `@govern.tool(intent="book", principal=lambda a: f'User::"{a["userId"]}"', context=lambda a: {"amount": a["amount"], "limit": a["limit"]})`; TS `govern.tool(fn, { intent, principal, resource, context })` — each of `principal`/`resource`/`context` is a value or a function of the call args. The `context` function may be **async** (return an awaitable/promise): it is awaited BEFORE the decision, so a value that takes a round trip — a quota read from a durable store with `counters_async`/`countersAsync` — is part of the context the policy evaluates. Python: an async `context` binding requires an `async def` tool body (on a sync body it is refused fail-closed with `TypeError` and nothing is authorized); TS tools are already async, so both forms work. The binding is resolved once per call, before the decision and before the re-decision an approval triggers. `authorize` takes an ALREADY-RESOLVED mapping in both lanes: an unresolved awaitable/promise raises `UnresolvedContextError` (`UNRESOLVED_CONTEXT_MESSAGE`, a `TypeError` subclass in both lanes) before anything reaches the engine and writes NO decision record — previously `dict(coroutine)`/`{...promise}` produced an empty context, so the call read as an ordinary Deny. Policies can then gate on `context.amount <= context.limit` and `principal == User::"..."`. (Only the DE-supported Cedar operators resolve: `context.*`, `==`, `is`, `like`, set `.contains()`.)
- **Low-level primitive:** Python `govern.authorize(action=, principal=, resource=, context=, approval=)`, TS `govern.authorize({ action, principal?, resource?, context?, approval? })` → `{decision: "Allow"|"Deny"|"NeedsApproval", allowed, needs_approval, approved, decision_id, reason}`. `decision_id` (the engine `request_id`) is also written to the audit line — join it to your own booking/order/record.
- **Obligations on an Allow:** a `permit` annotated `@obligate_redact("ssn, dob")` / `@obligate_max_items("25")` / `@obligate_log_values("false")` / any other `@obligate_<name>("raw")` yields `obligations` on the result — Python `result["obligations"] = {"redact": [...], "max_items": n, "log_values": bool, "extra": {name: [raw, ...]}}`, TS `d.obligations = { redact, maxItems, logValues, extra: Record<string, string[]> }` (each key only when set; the whole field absent when none). Constraints the caller MUST honour (strip those fields, cap the batch, don't log values) — typically in `on_result` / `onResult`. **Only an Allow carries them** (an approved one included); `Deny` and `NeedsApproval` never do. Every carrier — the engine's merged `details.obligations` and each determining permit's `policy_results[].obligations` — merges to the strictest reading: `redact` union, `max_items` min, `log_values` AND; `extra` values are raw and uninterpreted, so `extra[name]` lists every distinct value (sorted) and your code decides what a disagreement means. A known obligation the SDK cannot read (e.g. `max_items: "8"`) is never dropped: `authorize` raises/throws `AuthorizeError` with the fixed message `"invalid obligations on an Allow decision"` and a governed tool body does not run. Values are policy-authored strings — never derived from request or result data. Treat a missing obligation as no permission, not no limit (`maxItems ?? 0`). Requires `@watchlight/engine` / `watchlight-engine` >= 0.2.0 (the SDK's dependency); an older engine emits no field at all.
- **Human-in-the-loop:** a permit annotated `@enforcement_effect("require_approval")` yields **NeedsApproval** (not Allow/Deny). Get a human confirmation, then `mint_approval(action=, resource=)` (Python) / `govern.mintApproval({ action, resource })` (TS) → a single-use, TTL, resource-bound token; re-authorize with `approval=token` / `{ approval }` to proceed. `govern.tool(..., on_needs_approval=)` / `{ onNeedsApproval }` runs this inline. Fail-closed: unconfirmed → raises `NeedsApproval` (Python) / throws `NeedsApproval` (TS); the body never runs. DE tokens are local HMAC; Enterprise KMS-signs them into signed lineage.
- **Approval-token scope — BOTH defaults are per-process.** (a) The signing key is a random per-process key: a token cannot cross a process boundary and a restart invalidates every outstanding approval. Set `approval_secret=` / `approvalSecret` (or `$WATCHLIGHT_APPROVAL_SECRET`, or the existing `signing_secret` / `signingSecret`) — one value configures both kinds of token, under separate keys. Minimum 16 bytes; shorter raises `ApprovalError("weak_secret")` at construction. (b) "Used once" is recorded in an in-process map, so behind two replicas the same token can be consumed once on EACH. Pass `approval_store=` / `approvalStore`. The contract is ONE method, `add(id, expires_at)` (`expiresAt`), which MUST be an ATOMIC CHECK-AND-SET returning `True` when the reservation was new and `False` when the id was already present — an insert that fails on a duplicate key, `SET key val NX PXAT <expiresAt>`. A read (`has`) followed by an unconditional write CANNOT enforce single use: `consume` is async in TS, so anything between check and write is a window in which N concurrent consumes of one token are all approved (a single agent fanning out parallel tool calls after one confirmation). `has(id)` is optional and never consulted when consuming. Sync in both lanes, additionally promise-returning in TS (raced against `DEFAULT_APPROVAL_STORE_TIMEOUT_MS` = 2000 ms; a store that never settles is REFUSED, not left hanging — Python relies on its client's own timeout). The id is `<exp>.<nonce>`, never the signature. Fail-closed in every direction: `False`, a raise/throw, a timeout, or a non-boolean return all refuse (reported once on stderr, no error text, no id). The DEFAULT in-process store is itself atomic, so within one process N parallel consumes of one token yield exactly one Allow; its only gap is that it is per-process. Every refusal — expired, tampered, wrong key, replayed, store failure — surfaces as the SAME `NeedsApproval` hold with the uniform `"approval required"` reason.
- **Signed payload.** The token is `<exp>.<nonce>.<hmac-sha256-hex>`; the signed bytes are `<utf8 len>:<field>` for `"watchlight-de:approval:v1"`, principal, action, resource, exp, nonce, concatenated. Length prefixes make the fields unambiguous, so no two different `(principal, action, resource)` triples can sign the same bytes; the version marker means a token minted under a different payload format is refused rather than reinterpreted. Both lanes sign identical bytes, so a token minted by either package verifies in the other under the same secret. **Breaking in 0.8.0:** approval tokens minted by an earlier version do not verify against 0.8.0 (they were signed under the previous, space-joined payload). Nothing else changes; the tokens are short-lived, so drain in-flight approvals across the upgrade.

## Govern what a tool RETURNS — egress hook (Python + TS)

- `@govern.tool(intent, ..., on_result=hook)` (Python) / `govern.tool(fn, { intent, onResult })` (TS): `hook(result, info)` runs AFTER the body returns and BEFORE the caller sees the result, with `info = {intent, resource, principal, decision_id, obligations}` (TS `{ intent, resource, principal, decisionId, obligations? }`) — the SAME id written on the call's decision record, plus the obligations of that decision — the key is present only when the Allow carries any (both lanes; Python: read it with `info.get("obligations")`). `governTool` / `governTools` and the `governedHooks` `PostToolUse` hook populate it the same way. Use it to `sanitize`, screen, honour the obligations, or run a second `authorize` on the result's classification (e.g. `action: "release"`, `context: { classification }`). **Return a value → it replaces the payload; return `None` / `undefined` / `null` → passthrough; raise/throw → the payload is withheld (fail-closed): the error propagates, the raw result is never returned.** Python: an async hook requires an async tool body (on a sync body it is refused fail-closed with `TypeError`, payload withheld). Writes a value-free `egress` audit record `{ts, agent, principal, intent, event: "egress", resource, replaced, decision_id}` (+ `withheld: true` on a throw/timeout) — never the result. No hook → no record.
- Same option on the TS adapters: `governTool(tool, { intent, onResult })` / `governTools(tools, { onResult })`; `governedHooks({ onResult, onResultTimeoutMs? })` installs a Claude Agent SDK `PostToolUse` hook — a returned value becomes `updatedToolOutput` (what the model sees); a throw, or outrunning the internal deadline (default 8000 ms; the SDK matcher `timeout` is set to `ceil(ms/0.8)` s so ours fires first), replaces the output with the opaque `"not authorized"`. Joined to the PreToolUse decision by `tool_use_id`; without one, no `decision_id` on the egress record. Pattern: `examples/patterns/egress-after-read.md`.

## Redact PII before an agent reads a document (sanitize, 0.3.0 — Python + TS)

- `govern.sanitize(text, ...)` (Python) / `govern.sanitize(text, {...})` (TS) — deterministic redaction on **extracted text** (extract a PDF/DOCX to text first; never hand the agent the original file — its hidden layers leak). Detects EMAIL, PHONE, SSN, CREDIT_CARD (Luhn-validated), IBAN, IPV4, API_KEY, PASSPORT (labelled numbers + MRZ lines), DOB (labelled dates of birth) — `DETECTOR_VERSION = "de-rules-2"`. `known: [...]` / `known=[...]` redacts an app-supplied dictionary of exact values (case-insensitive, every occurrence, counted as KNOWN; values never leave the process). PERSON and ADDRESS are opt-in, lower-precision heuristics (off by default; list them in `types`). Modes: `tag` (consistent `<EMAIL_1>`, default), `mask` (`[EMAIL]`), `hash`. Returns the redacted text + a **value-free** report (counts by type + mode — never the values), and writes a value-free `sanitization` audit record. Pass `decision_id=` (Python) / `{ decisionId }` (TS) from the `authorize` decision that governed the read: it is echoed on the report and written as `decision_id` on the `sanitization` audit line, so it joins the decision's line on the same key (opaque, 1–128 chars — UTF-16 code units in TS, code points in Python — no control or line-separator characters; otherwise `SanitizeError`). Pass `principal=` / `{ principal }` — who the text is sanitized FOR, the Cedar principal exactly as written on the decision record — and it is echoed on the report and written as `principal` on the `sanitization` line, under the same key the decision line uses: the record then answers "what was redacted, for whom" on its own, including when the sanitization runs BEFORE any decision exists to join to. Same validation and error type as `decision_id`; an identifier the CALLER supplies, never anything derived from the content; a record without it is unchanged. Fail-closed. A pure `sanitize(...)` is also exported; recall is bounded by the enabled detectors.

## Screen retrieved content before it reaches the model (screen — Python + TS)

- `govern.screen(text, ...)` (Python) / `govern.screen(text, {...})` (TS) — deterministic, rule-based detection of prompt-injection / output-leak shapes in text the agent reads but did not write (web pages, search and tool results) or in what the model produced. Seven families, each a named counter in the report: `INSTRUCTION_OVERRIDE`, `ROLE_SWITCH`, `PROMPT_EXFILTRATION`, `JAILBREAK_MARKER`, `AUTHORITY_IMPERSONATION`, `HTML_INJECTION`, `PROMPT_LEAK`. Modes: `report` (default — text untouched, counts only), `redact` (matched spans → `[FAMILY]`). Report is **value-free**: `{mode, detector_version ("de-screen-1"), counts, total, flagged}` — never the matched text or offsets; writes a value-free `screening` audit record. Pass `decision_id=` (Python) / `{ decisionId }` (TS) from the `authorize` decision that governed the read: it is echoed on the report and written as `decision_id` on the `screening` line, so it joins the decision (same bounds as `sanitize`: opaque, 1–128 chars, no control characters — otherwise `ScreenError`). `principal=` / `{ principal }` works exactly as it does on `sanitize`: validated the same way, echoed on the report and written as `principal` on the `screening` line. Fail-closed (`ScreenError` with fixed messages on a non-string, unknown mode / family, empty family list, or a malformed `decision_id` / `principal`). Matching ignores case, whitespace runs and zero-width characters; it does NOT decode leetspeak, homoglyphs or encodings, and text that quotes an attack verbatim is flagged. `redact` marks the trigger (a whole `<script>…</script>` element when its body has no `<`) — it does not neutralise HTML; markers can be spoofed by input, so decide from the report, not the text. Call it inside the governed tool body before returning (throw `Denied(toolName, intent, DENY_REASON)` to refuse), or in the `onResult` / `on_result` egress hook of `govern.tool`. Known TS/Python divergence: Turkish dotted capital İ case-folds only in Python. Pattern: [screen-before-model](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/patterns/screen-before-model.md).

## TypeScript / Node lane — `@watchlight/sdk` (verified, 0.8.0)

- `import { govern, Denied, NeedsApproval } from "@watchlight/sdk";` — same default governor, fail-closed, value-free `.watchlight/audit.jsonl`. `govern.tool(fn, {intent})` is a **higher-order function** (not a decorator) and returns an async function.
- `govern.allow('permit(...);')` / `govern.load("policies.json")`; `govern.tool(fn, { intent, principal?, resource?, context?, onNeedsApproval?, onResult? })`; `govern.authorize({...})`; `govern.mintApproval({...})`; `govern.sanitize(text, {...})`; `govern.screen(text, {...})`; `govern.counters({...})` / `await govern.countersAsync({...})`. Governor options: `new Watchlight({ agent?, auditDir?, auditSink?, signingSecret?, approvalSecret?, approvalStore?, counterSource?, apdpUrl?, token?, tenantId? })`.
- **The signing secret** (`signing_secret=` / `signingSecret`, `$WATCHLIGHT_SIGNING_SECRET`): signs scope tokens, and approval tokens unless `approval_secret` / `approvalSecret` overrides them. FORMER NAME `token_secret` / `tokenSecret` / `$WATCHLIGHT_TOKEN_SECRET` — still accepted at lower precedence, warns once per process; setting both names to DIFFERENT values raises at construction (`ScopeTokenError("mismatch")`), identical values are fine. Precedence: option `signing_secret` → `$WATCHLIGHT_SIGNING_SECRET` → option `token_secret` → `$WATCHLIGHT_TOKEN_SECRET` → unset (scope tokens fail closed; approvals fall back to a random per-process key). Every process that exchanges tokens needs the same value. Minimum 16 bytes per entry, enforced at construction; never logged, never in an error, never in the trail. **Rotation:** pass an ORDERED LIST (or a comma-separated env var), newest first — the first entry signs, every entry verifies. Two deploys: add the new secret at the front, wait out the longest token lifetime in flight (`ttl_seconds` of a scope token, `ttl_ms` of an approval), then drop the old one. A single-value change is an immediate cutover that invalidates every outstanding token. An empty list, or one whose entries are all blank, fails closed. Which entry verified a token is never reported. Guide: `docs/signing-secret.md`.
- Framework adapters: `governedHooks({ intentFor, onResult? })` → Claude Agent SDK `hooks` (PreToolUse gate; PostToolUse egress when `onResult` is set); `governTool(tool, { intent, onResult? })` / `governTools(tools, { intentFor, onResult? })` → LangChain / LangGraph.js `StructuredTool` governance. `govern.scope().attenuate()` → strict-subset sub-agent scopes (`DE_MAX_DEPTH` 5); `scope.toToken()` / `await govern.scopeFromToken(token)` carry a scope to another process (`new Watchlight({ signingSecret })` or `WATCHLIGHT_SIGNING_SECRET`; the receiving engine replays the chain; `ScopeTokenError` on a bad token, `AttenuationDenied` on a widened one).
- Graduation: set `WATCHLIGHT_APDP_URL` (+ `WATCHLIGHT_PLUGIN_TOKEN`, `WATCHLIGHT_TENANT_ID`) to run the same code against the networked control plane; `govern.mode` → `"in-process"` | `"networked"`.
- Packages: `@watchlight/sdk` (Apache-2.0 glue) depends on `@watchlight/engine` (the compiled engine). Node ≥ 18. Docs: https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/typescript

## Docs (narrative guides on docs.watchlight.ai/de)

- [Overview](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/): what DE is, the package map, and where it fits the progressive-deployment model.
- [Quickstart](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/quickstart): `pip install`, govern a tool, print your first ALLOW/DENY in under five minutes.
- [Using the governor](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/using-the-governor): where the governor lives in an application — construct once at start-up, how many you need, what every name shares, and the request-handler / worker / test shapes.
- [TypeScript / Node](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/typescript): `npm install @watchlight/sdk`, govern a tool in-process, runtime context + human-in-the-loop, Claude Agent SDK + LangGraph.js adapters.
- [Cedar policy syntax](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/policies): the policy language the engine evaluates, from first principles.
- [The identity model](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/identity-model): the subject principal (`User::"…"` / `Agent::"…"`), the reserved `context.actor` and `context.actor_chain` keys, and where each value comes from.
- [Glossary](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/glossary): every term the DE documentation uses, with the easy-to-confuse pairs contrasted.
- [The signing secret](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/signing-secret): which processes need the same value, what happens when it is missing, and how to rotate it in two deploys.
- [Governed agents (in-process)](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/governed-agents): govern an agent lifecycle with `InProcessClient` (from `watchlight-agent-sdk` / `watchlight_core`).
- [Sub-agent scope attenuation](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/scope-attenuation): strict-subset confinement, the depth-5 ceiling, and the deepagents example.
- [Govern an MCP server](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/mcp-server): `serve` (HTTP) and `serve_stdio` (stdio) transports.
- [Enforcement effects](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/enforcement-effects): what a policy can do beyond allow/deny.
- [Field reference](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/reference): the request/response shape and what is enforced vs advisory.
- [Developer Edition vs Enterprise](https://docs.watchlight.ai/de/comparison): what the control plane adds and when to reach for it.

## Runnable examples (in the repo)

- [agent.py](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/agent.py): the smallest governed agent — the DENY line, zero infra.
- [showcase/denied-before-execute](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/tree/main/examples/showcase/denied-before-execute): governed transfer against a stub bank with a call counter; a `forbid` above a threshold is refused before the body runs and the counter is asserted 0 (Python + TS; `policy.suite.json` doubles as the golden tests).
- [showcase/identity](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/tree/main/examples/showcase/identity) (`identity.py` + `identity.mjs`): the identity model end to end — ONE governor and ONE policy set, agents named with `as_()`/`as()` (policy count printed before and after to show renaming does not reload it), then the three cases side by side in one audit stream: agent alone (`principal` = `Agent::"flight-booker"`, no `actor_chain`), the same agent for a person (`User::"db:4412"`, same actor), and a sub-agent via `delegate()` (leaf `seat-picker`, chain `["flight-booker","seat-picker"]`, subject unchanged). Policies keyed on the subject, on `context.actor` and on `context.actor_chain.contains(...)`; the same call made FOUR ways to show where the actor comes from (base governor / `as()` / per-call `agent` override / `delegate()`) — renaming always yields a fresh single-element chain, only `delegate` appends; four refusals asserted (supplying `actor`, extending `actor_chain`, renaming a delegate, the per-call `agent` override on a delegate — each writing no record, each matched on the guard's message), while a context identical to the derived values is accepted; a verified token's `sub` claim and a local session row producing the identical call.
- [showcase/human-in-the-loop](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/tree/main/examples/showcase/human-in-the-loop): `NeedsApproval` → pending request on disk → separate `approve.py`/`approve.mjs` signs a grant → `resume` runs once with an `approved: true` record joined to the pending one; grant and token replays refused (Python + TS).
- [governed_research_agent.py](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/governed_research_agent.py): a multi-tool agent governed by intent.
- [governed_subagents.py](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/governed_subagents.py): scope attenuation — every child a strict subset of its parent.
- [governed_deepagents.py](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/governed_deepagents.py): governing a [deepagents](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents) deep agent via `govern.scope` (runs without an API key).
- [governed_langgraph_agent.py](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/governed_langgraph_agent.py) · [governed_pydantic_ai_agent.py](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/governed_pydantic_ai_agent.py) · [governed_claude_agent.py](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/governed_claude_agent.py): framework plugins, governed in-process.
- [governed_mcp_server.py](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/governed_mcp_server.py): a policy enforcement point in front of an MCP server.
- [context_governance.py](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/context_governance.py): policy-based content/PII screening.
- [showcase/policy-tests-ci/](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/tree/main/examples/showcase/policy-tests-ci): policy suites as a CI gate — a GitHub Actions workflow template running `watchlight policy test` (TypeScript and Python CLIs), plus a widened policy variant that fails the suite.
- [showcase/audit-forensics/](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/tree/main/examples/showcase/audit-forensics): reconstruct who did what from `audit.jsonl` — generators for a trail with every record kind, `forensics.py` and jq recipes that join on `decision_id`; exact field names per record kind.
- [showcase/poisoned-rag/](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/showcase/poisoned-rag/README.md) (`rag.py` + `rag.mjs`): a RAG pipeline where one retrieved document hides a prompt injection and personal data — `screen()` withholds it in the `on_result` hook, the permit's `@obligate_redact` obligation drives `sanitize()` for what passes, and decision / screening / sanitization / egress records join on one `decision_id`; self-asserting, exits non-zero on failure.
- [showcase/web-backend/](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/showcase/web-backend/README.md) (`app.py` + `app.mjs`, `check.py` + `check.mjs`): a FastAPI and an Express backend with one governed endpoint — the bearer-authenticated user becomes the per-call `principal` (`User::"<user>"`), the policy is scoped to that user and account, denials are an opaque 403, and the check script starts the server on an ephemeral 127.0.0.1 port, drives it and asserts every decision record carries the acting user; FastAPI/uvicorn and Express are optional extras (`requirements.txt` / `package.json` in the folder), not dependencies of the packages.
- [showcase/red-team/](https://github.com/watchlight-ai-beacon/watchlight-de/blob/main/examples/showcase/red-team/README.md) (`run.py` + `run.mjs`, `corpus.json`): 30 synthetic adversarial prompts in 10 families — the seven `SCREEN_FAMILIES` (must be withheld by the `screen()` hook on a governed `ingest`), two policy-caught request families (must be denied by policy), and a `BENIGN` control — with per-family counts of withheld / reached / denied / executed; exits non-zero on any miss and on a family neither layer handles (`corpus.unhandled.json` demonstrates).
- Policy files live beside them: `watchlight.policy.json`, `research.policy.json`, `framework.policy.json`, `mcp.policy.json`.

## Gotchas for coding agents (get these right)

- **Fail-closed.** No policy = every governed call is denied. You must `govern.load(...)` or `govern.allow(...)` a permit before anything runs.
- **A `@govern.tool` resource is `tool/<function_name>`.** Write policies against that resource, e.g. `permit(principal, action == Action::"research", resource == Resource::"tool/web_search");` — or leave `resource` unconstrained.
- **Framework plugins authorize as `Agent::"<uuid>"`, not your run label.** A policy that pins `principal == User::"research-agent"` will NOT match a plugin-governed run and every action is denied. Gate framework-agent policies on the **action/resource**, or on `principal is Agent` — never a hardcoded principal id you can't know in advance. (The low-level `InProcessClient.authorize("research-agent", ...)` DOES use the label you pass — that's the one place a `User::"..."` principal matches.)
- **`serve()` fronts HTTP MCP servers; `serve_stdio()` fronts stdio ones.** Never pass a `stdio://` string as `upstream_url` to `serve()`: on `watchlight-mcp >= 0.2.1` it is rejected at startup with a clear error; on earlier versions it binds and then fails as a late 502 on the first allowed call. Use `serve_stdio(upstream_command=[...])` for a stdio-launched server.
- **`watchlight dev` needs a free port (default 7000); `serve()` needs its listen port free.** DE keeps no process registry — you own port hygiene. A stale orphaned server can hold a port and silently produce an empty audit.
- **Cedar string idioms:** the engine resolves `context.*`, `==`, `is`, `like` (glob), and `set.contains()`. It does **not** have `.startsWith()` / `.contains()` on strings — use `like "prefix*"`. Entity-attribute reads and `in` hierarchy are not part of the DE engine surface; a policy that relies on them silently denies.
- **`context.actor` is reserved.** The SDK sets it on every authorize; a differing caller value raises `ReservedContextError` rather than being overwritten. Use it for agent-scoped rules — `when { context.actor == "…" }` — and keep `principal` for the subject. **Breaking in 0.8.0**, alongside the typed principal and the approval-token payload: an application that already used `actor` (or `actor_chain`) for a value of its OWN now raises at the call site. The migration is a rename — move that value to a key of your own (`context.requested_by`) and update the policies that read it. There is no opt-out flag and there will not be one: a flag that let a caller supply the key would make every `context.actor` rule forgeable while it was on.
- **An omitted `principal` is `Agent::"<agent-name>"`, not a bare name.** Anything that string-matched the old bare value in the audit trail (a dashboard, a `counters(principal=…)` key) must use the typed form. An agent-scoped policy written against another entity type — `principal == User::"<agent-name>"` — used to match the untyped substitution and now denies; spell it `Agent::"<name>"` or match `context.actor`.
- **An entity type the engine does not know (e.g. `Service::"x"`) refuses the call**: `AuthorizeRequestError` (fixed message `REQUEST_INVALID_MESSAGE`), audited as a Deny, body never runs. Principal types: `User`, `Agent`, `Group`, `Role`, `Tool`, `Resource`, `Workflow`.
- **Audit is value-free by contract.** Argument *values* never enter `.watchlight/audit.jsonl` — only who, what intent, which resource, and the decision. Don't expect to read tool arguments back out of it.
